title: Amnesty International reports on borderization along the administrative boundary lines
body:
In July 2019 Amnesty International published a report and press release on what is called borderization, the building of barriers along the administrative boundary lines (ABL) separating Georgia from Abkhazia and from South Ossetia (the Tskhinvali Region). Russian forces and the de facto authorities have built barbed wire, fences and ditches along the line. Russian forces have been stationed in both regions without Georgia's consent since the August 2008 conflict. Amnesty said the process began in 2011.

According to Georgian authorities, as of late 2018 at least 34 villages had been divided by fences, and an estimated 800 to 1,000 families had lost access to their agricultural land. Amnesty said hundreds of people are detained each year for crossing outside designated points, which the Russian and de facto authorities consider illegal. The Khurcha crossing, a former trade hub, closed in March 2017.

Amnesty described individual cases. Davit Vanishvili, aged 85, of Khurvaleti was given a choice in 2013 to stay on the South Ossetian side or move; he stayed, and he and relatives risk detention when crossing the fence to reach his pension and medicine. Amiran Gugutishvili, aged 71, of Gugutiankari lost access to his apple orchard in 2017. The findings drew on about 150 testimonies from field trips in March and July 2018 and June 2019. Amnesty wrote to Russia, the de facto authorities and Georgia; only Georgia responded.
